comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C54-C58 regarding MHT formulation analyses. Both accept the null findings after FDR correction and the uncorrected exploratory findings. OpenEval notes appropriate caution needed for uncorrected results, while peer reviewers praise the detailed approach to obtaining MHT prescription data.

Perfect agreement on claim C61 regarding sensitivity analyses. Both find the exclusion of participants with brain-affecting diagnoses strengthens confidence in main findings. Peer reviewers specifically praise this as a methodological strength.

Perfect agreement on claims C93-C96 regarding study limitations (UK Biobank biases, healthy volunteer effect, lack of diversity). Both accept these as important limitations that reduce generalizability. Peer reviewers note the authors appropriately acknowledged these weaknesses.

Strong agreement on methodological claims C97-C105 (quality control, exclusion criteria) and sample description claims C37-C39. Both find the methodology appropriate and well-justified. Peer reviewers praise the large population-based sample and comprehensive details, while OpenEval notes procedures enhance data quality.

Strong agreement on claims C52-C53 regarding surgical history findings. Both accept that MHT users with surgical menopause showed younger brain age than non-users. Peer reviewers praise consideration of menopause type as a strength, while OpenEval notes observational design limits causal inference.

Strong agreement on claims C73-C76 regarding demographic differences between groups (age, education, health behaviors). Both accept these as important confounders that complicate interpretation. OpenEval and peer reviewers both note these are appropriately discussed rather than invalidating findings.

Agreement on claim C59 regarding APOE ε4 main effect on brain measures. Both accept this well-established finding without challenge. Peer reviewers note examination of genetic risk factors as a strength.

Agreement on claim C60 regarding null APOE ε4 × MHT interactions. Both accept the lack of interaction effects. OpenEval notes this contrasts with some previous studies but is appropriately corrected for multiple comparisons. Peer reviewers accept the null interaction clearly.

Strong agreement on claims C42-C45 regarding primary findings that current MHT users show higher brain age gap and smaller hippocampal volumes. Both find these robust primary results well-supported by statistical analyses. Peer reviewers describe findings as 'convincing' with no methodological concerns.

Agreement on claims C46-C47 regarding null findings for past MHT users. Both accept this distinction between current and past users. Editor explicitly acknowledges current but not past users showed adverse effects.

Agreement on claim C48 regarding null finding for age at MHT initiation. Both accept this null result without challenge. Peer reviewers implicitly accept by noting study's strength in examining timing, while OpenEval notes this is important for understanding timing effects.

Strong agreement on claims C49-C50 regarding positive associations of MHT duration and age at last use with adverse brain measures. Both accept these findings as valid and important. Peer reviewers explicitly summarize these associations without raising concerns.

Agreement on claims C64-C69 summarizing duration and timing findings. Both accept these as valid summary statements of the study's main results regarding longer duration and older age at last use being associated with adverse brain health measures.

Agreement on claims C62-C63, C72 summarizing primary findings about current MHT use and brain measures. Both accept these summary statements. Peer reviewers describe findings as 'convincing' and note the incorporation of brain age estimate as a strength.

Agreement on claim C71 regarding the main conclusion that associations vary by duration and surgical history. Both accept this appropriately cautious conclusion. Peer reviewers explicitly endorse this statement, noting interpretations are reasonable.
Agreement on claim C70 regarding surgical history modifying MHT effects. Both accept this finding as part of the study's main conclusions about variation by surgical history.

Agreement on claims C40-C41 regarding age differences between MHT users and non-users. Both accept these demographic differences as statistically significant and important for interpretation. Peer reviewers treat these as important context.
Agreement on claims C37-C39 describing the study sample characteristics. Both accept the sample description as appropriate. Peer reviewers praise the large population-based sample as a strength.
